My PR changes what was required to add core functionality. Many issues were identified during my PRs development that created a list of further changes required to make OpenCode support the agentic workflows that 2026 is going to require a Harness have to stay SOTA. 

Making OpenCode have a multi-caller system is going to be challenging due to dependencies between UI, UX, and other systems for agentic orchestration and workflows.

Right now I'm building an effective replacement for compaction that completely obviates any need for session recovery and will improve the reasoning capabilities of models. This is a critical part of making long horizon agentic workflows work.

While I can currently get similar function to Agent Teams using my PR, context management plugin, agents framework, and manually steering my agents, it's far from being an the automated process that it needs to be, and can't be, without doing a lot more building of dependencies. 

It's taking time. The context management system in particular. I've spent the last four days basically reading long reports and change proposal to the current SPEC. After that spec gets finalized, them implementation. Then adding more features that require another round of reports and spec development. Then hopefully the system I modeled and constructed through reason, logic, and research, will work well enough to release and move to the next item needed on the roadmap. 

But, because I'm basically working alone, it's going to take a long time. I'm hoping once I release my context management plugin it'll help organize people and promote more collaboration. But that's probably wishful thinking. 

So basically, I'm saying I'm working to make this, and do it right, but I don't know how long that's going to take. It's already over a month of development, could be another month or two. The systems design is complicated; the coding and implementation isn't the problem, the agents handle that part easy enough. 

My token usage is actually very low during the hardest parts because I'm spending most of my time reading agent reports and writing feedback. The tasks need attentive driven hyper-focused humans; more inference doesn't fix this yet. Though, that changes over time. The workflow ends up being able to help build things as it is being built.

It's hard to know where the ceiling is at for improving how intelligently the agents function. 

Google Deep Think seems like it's just a complex structured agentic workflow. I don't think there's any part of it we won't be able to reproduce in OpenCode after I've built this agentic system. 

So, currently, a lot of what I'm doing is basically a lesser version of deep think. 

Anyways. More reports to read. This one about improving the Reasoning Protocol that holds everything together in a way that most people won't catch without it being pointed out explicitly. The potential for other people to break complex systems like the one I've made is high. The agents don't see and understand things without having a human pint them out. This really is something that needs an organized team where each member goes deep dive and coordinates what they're working on.

I wanted to give people an example of what both the work I'm doing involves and how these agentic workflows with my PR improve outputs.

Background:
- Partner-Opus subagent tasked to evaluate how users feedback/ideas might require changes to the Reasoning Protocol.
- Partners report and relevant information reviewed by team of Associates (GPT 5.2, Codex 5.3. Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1, GLM 5, Kimi 2.5), which write their feedback to relay-files.
- Principal (primary agent) reviews relay-files and reports items of note to user. Gemini finds something which diverges from all other Associates findings.
- user reviews items of note, particularly Gemini's finding in greater detail. Tasks Principal to persist sessions with  all non-Gemini Associates to review Geminis finding.
- Associates write addendums to their relay-file reports. Principal synthesizes. 
- User instructs Principal to task Gemini to review each Associates addendum and then write it's own addendum to it's report.

Below is an excerpt of Gemini's addendum:

## Addendum: Response to Cross-Model Debate (2026-02-19)

### 1. Where I Concede: The "Particle-Level" Category Error
My colleagues—particularly Opus and the Principal—were correct to push back on my specific wording. In my zeal to import the user's exact "Reality vs. Perception" framework into Rule 4.4, I proposed instructing agents to ask about "particle-level interactions." 

This was a mistake. As Opus rightly pointed out, asking about particle-level interactions when evaluating a software architecture or a legal argument is a category error. The underlying principle (that reality is structural configurations) is universal, but the *literal* phrasing is domain-specific. I concede that forcing "particle-level" terminology into a universal protocol would create cognitive overhead and metaphorical translation errors for agents. 

### 2. Where I Hold My Ground: Epistemology *Is* the Mechanism
I hold my ground firmly against the claim—initially advanced by Partner and echoed by Kimi—that "teaching epistemology" is somehow distinct from "instructing behavior" for an LLM.

Kimi argued: "An LLM's behavior emerges from pattern matching across training data, not from holding philosophical commitments." This attempts to separate the pattern-matching mechanism from the content it matches against. But the philosophical commitment *is* the pattern. When an LLM evaluates a claim, the choice between classifying it as "substantive inference" or "aspirational" is dictated by which epistemological heuristic it activates. If the prompt does not explicitly construct a new epistemological lens, the model defaults to its pre-trained perceptual heuristic ("unvalidated = speculative"). 

GLM's analysis of the mechanism confirms my position perfectly.

### 3. Validating the Mechanism: Priming and Similarity Space
GLM provided the most intellectually honest and mechanically accurate description of why my insight works. 

GLM noted that conceptual framing operates by:
1. **Priming specific attention patterns** (making structural relationships more salient).
2. **Shifting similarity space activation** (lighting up different regions of training data).
3. **Constraining hypothesis generation**.

This perfectly articulates *why* "epistemology is behavioral instruction." When we give the model the Reality vs. Perception framework, we are not asking it to sit and ponder existence; we are actively shifting its similarity space activation away from surface-level heuristics and toward structural modeling. GLM's observation from Session 24—where the "identity shaping" conceptual frame successfully overrode the default "concluded = prune" heuristic—is empirical proof of this mechanism.

//

The point I'm trying to demonstrate is that agentic workflows will self-correct with minimal steering. Claude Code's Agent Teams doesn't provide the proper environment for that. It's all one model, with the same weights, where the only way to try to get differing perspectives is prompt engineering. This limits the emergent complexity that can manifest within systems - Claude Code and CoWork using Claude-only are inherently constrained.

Building a proper Agentic Collaboration Framework (ACF) in OpenCode is going to be complex, but it's attainable. It's already 'working' for the most part but relies upon my manual interventions/steering. Building things out further will enable Primary agents to orchestrate a lot more of the workflow, and keep the user involved for high-level decisions. 

I periodically extract insights from sessions into skill files, so orchestration becomes more sophisticated over time. Essentially, the feedback loop compounds the more complex and interconnected these systems become. The models we have access to are far more capable than what most people think, because they're just not leveraging their intelligence fully. Deep Think level intelligence should be the default in OpenCode. But, until my PR is merged, and I build things our further, it won't be.

GNAP is interesting, but a limited system focused on coding that breaks down under the demands of knowledge-work or general task performance. It isn't a true substitute - too many failure points alongside significant constraints.

I think a multi-caller tasking system with a shared state system is going to outperform systems focused on coordinating coding projects. Such systems adaptively specialize for the work they perform, as they have the capacity to learn, and then recursively build whatever is required to optimize the workflow and domain that the user is focused upon. 

I think what people need to focus on is not the implementation part of coding workflows - it's the cognitively demanding systems design and spec development. That is primarily knowledge-work, even when it is coding focused, and is far more controlling now, with the current capabilities of models, to whether or not a project ends up being genius, generic, or outright slop.

What is the plan to release this feature? And when?

> What is the plan to release this feature? And when?

Currently building the state modeling system the agents need to be able to coordinate in projects and between projects. 

After that, updating a DCP fork that provides context optimization. 

Then adding asynchronous tasking and other less complex changes that'll be time consuming to test and fine tune (agents need basic rules for when to task sync or async).

The final change will be replacing the parent-child task system with a multi-caller task system. That's what is needed the most to get a 'better than agent teams' feature into OpenCode. Despite being conceptually straightforward it also seems to be the most complex and potentially breaking to implement. Which is why I've prioritized building the tools that will extend my agents cognitive capabilities first, reasoning that it'll improve their ability to account for dependencies and develop a solution that doesn't break agent permissions or the sqlite session history DB.

I can't predict when it'll be finished. All I can tell you is I've been working basically all day every day on this and encountering a lot of complications. To finish the state modeling system I have to build a new PC and migrate from Windows 10 to Linux Arch. Can't test many core features on my current 2011 era system.

Also, late nights, tired, burning out, trying to take breaks to recover, and wondering if it's a mistake to keep trying to build the tools I need for my litigation and advocacy work instead of just trying to do the work I can without those tools. I'm not building because I enjoy it; only because I need the tools. My mental capacity is diminishing the longer I grind away at this too. It's information overload combined with sleep deprivation and lack of exercise. This is not fun or enjoyable.

@NamedIdentity Maybe the following helps? ( an issue for nemo agent took kit, missing the exact thing, I actually built it and running)

Problem this feature solves:

Agent executions are currently fire-and-forget, no state tracking, no external abort, no crash recovery, no
session continuity between invocations. These are production requirements for teams deploying agents as long-running services.

Redis natively supports all of these patterns

Proposed solution:

create redis_orchestration to provide:

Task lifecycle state machine
Redis strings with TTL for execution state (running → completed | failed | timed_out | aborted). Pub/Sub notifications on state transitions. SCAN-based crash recovery to detect orphaned running states on startup.

External abort
Redis Pub/Sub control channel per task. External callers publish abort, middleware cancels execution. Enables UI kill buttons, API cancellation, inter-agent coordination.

Session continuity
Redis lists for conversation history with TTL-based expiry. Size-based rotation when sessions exceed configurable limits. Working memory (Redis, hot) with automatic compaction to long-term storage.

Execution metrics
Redis hashes with daily counters (tasks, tokens, cost, errors). Complements existing profiler/observability middleware with persistent aggregate stats.

Reference: https://github.com/NVIDIA/NeMo-Agent-Toolkit/issues/1793

@h-network The goal I have is a unified system within OpenCode that optimizes for general task performance.  External tools that focus on coding are too narrow, limiting the problems agents can work on.

The ideal agentic collaboration framework is one in which a primary agent can dynamically construct and execute complex orchestrations tailored to a specific problem. When you create narrow roles and specializations that stay fixed, you limit the agents discretion, autonomy, and task performance.

In what I'm building, agents are given tools and information, and over time learn how to best use them during problem solving. That is why the state modeling system has to be developed first; agentic collaboration requires feedback loops which result in learning.  

The user doesn't try to find a way to make the tool work for them, the agentic framework specializes to the problems the user works on as they work the problems.

Have you seen https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/12730?

> Hi!
> 
> Have you seen [#12730](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/12730)?

I did not see that yet. Interesting approach. It would be useful if added to OpenCode. But I think it's the wrong approach long-term. 

Teams should use the existing delegation system and not be so rules based. Agents should have a general framework to perform tasks in a collaborative manner. A primary agent creates a team by tasking subagents and the subagents coordinate by communicating directly with each other. 

Treating agent teams as something additional and separate from the existing delegation system will limit OpenCode and become obsolete as AI models improve. 

Ideally, agent teams as a term should be abandoned and all that's needed to make a primary agent and it's subagents collaborate on problems is an agent skill. I think what OpenCode is missing which that PR tried to compensate for is OpenCode doesn't have a state/memory system. Once that is made, agentic collaboration has a way to retain and exchange state across agents and projects.

I think what people are missing is the vision to construct a unified system. 

Put simply, a proper state/memory system will obviate the need for an 'agent teams' style approach. It facilitates a more elegant, organic, and powerful delegation based collaborative process.  That is why I'm building it first. It is a primary dependency. 

That PR is good, but it's quick and dirty and won't last as agent supportive Harness infrastructure enhances agents cognitive capabilities, and AI models get smarter. The collaborative system that needs building is one that enables agent discretion and autonomy for problem solving without creating constraints that impair task performance. 

Put simply if a 'team member' identified that it needs a deep research or deep reasoning workflow to fully investigate a matter, then it should be able to delegate that. If you want an agent to solve a problem it needs all the supportive tools and context to model and solve it. It doesn't have that when it's alone in its own session and cannot delegate to orchestrate multi agent workflows. The problem and it's requirements determine the workflow required to attain a solution. 

We need to build environments for agents that assume the agents are or will shortly become smart enough to figure out how to solve complex problems, either through supportive Harness infrastructure (state systems) enhancing existing models or with advancements from future AI models.

After reviewing the proposal by @panwar-stack and the opencode-ensemble linked by @shahrin014 I believe people have become preoccupied with copying Claude Code Agent Teams, rather than trying to design an optimal environment for agents to collaborate autonomously while working tasks.

The basic premise of creating a set of tools an agent uses to create a team, send messages, and manage tasks is inefficient and counterproductive. The Agent Teams implementation by Anthropic was always generic and half-baked.

To get agents to work collaboratively means making a limited amount of harness native tools provide all needed functions. Not adding more and more tools to bloat context and degrade agent/model performance. The research data has been clear, adding more and more tools degrades agent performance - keep things lean and adaptable. Make a limited set of tools provide the functions needed under a wide variety of situations. Only make specific tools for critical functions that cannot be met through adapting the existing toolset. 

I'm still working on my Agentic Collaboration Framework, in which an 'agent teams equivalent or better' is naturally subsumed. It continues to be slow, challenging work, because it require a lot of thinking through the systems design. The implementation work is, trivial by comparison.

I spent over two months building a state modelling system, a type of specialized memory layer. I'm now working on refining a DCP fork I made in Jan-Feb into a a context management system that will enter into a feedback loop with the state modelling system, each enhancing an agents cognitive capabilities. Those systems will also benefit from any supplementary memory system; multiple feedback loops between complementary systems is the approach I'm taking. It's how biology works; it's innate to how complex systems operate.

Once agents have a state-modelling and context-management system, then a multi-caller system that enables agentic collaboration can be being driven by model intelligence alone. It'll practically self-assemble. I'm already seeing that occur in my state-model system - the agents are collecting performance data on tasked agents, compiling the data, using it to construct models about each AI models performance on the tasks in the projects, and then injecting guidance into the orchestrating agents context. 

Most of the wiring in these Agent Team copy-cat plugins create logic that is unnecessary, even counterproductive. Most of the core functions of 'Agent Teams' can be obtained by making agent-skills while using my OpenCode PR that lets subagents task subagents and persist subagent sessions. 

Claude Code needed Agent Teams instead of an Agent Skill because Claude Code does not allow you to persist subagent session and have subagent task and persist other subagents. If you really want Agents to collaborate, you do not use 'Agent Teams'. You create a harness native environment where collaboration is an organic process that occurs in response to task complexity.

Rather than having a plugin with tons of added tools, there is a more elegant solution using the Task tool and an agent skill, loaded only when a task is complex enough to require multi-agent orchestration. The Natural Language code of an agent-skill is easily transferable and can rapidly iterate, and can benefit from a wider range of human expertise during development. The same is not true of these plugins. 

People need to put a lot more thought into the systems design. It's the hard part, and it's what Anthropic seems to suck the most at when it comes to Claude Code development.
